articles.fullContent: Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving, and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed. Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest. But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering. It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future: It needs to be possible to formally verify code that runs in any environment, from web browsers down to embedded systems. Industry engineers need to know provably correct code is even possible and be comfortable enough with it to at least tell their LLMs to write it. Those industry engineers must be able to reason about formal correctness properties enough to even know the right things are being proven. In the words of Leonardo de Moura (opens new window): Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate. This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions. § The long winding road of Magmide My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal. I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window): It didn't make sense to build a new proof assistant when Lean has been making such rapid progress. An assembly-level language was insanely difficult and wasn't necessary to gain adoption from practitioners. I didn't have the appetite to pursue some strained business model for a project that ultimately makes most sense as a pure public good. So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would: Compile to WebAssembly using the Garbage Collection (opens new window) features.

articles.fullContent: The icon indicates free access to the linked research on JSTOR. In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships, so huge they were referred to as “floating cities,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves. The disaster quickly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage, the “right of wreck.” It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.” That said, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord. In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.) Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling. Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter). Lonely Diarist of the High Seas July 21, 2025 As ship stewardess, Ella Sheldon tended to upper-crust women onboard and battled a range of workplace demons. Her journals tell her story. The resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee. Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective. In 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “man, dog, or cat” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat) Legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. Still, people could be rough in their efforts to “salvage.” In Estonia, for instance, where the local lords were entitled to rewards if they helped to save ships in distress, people developed a habit of launching into enthusiastic “rescue” operations, whether or not there was any real danger. articles.fullContent: I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around

articles.fullContent: Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan. Image Kamil Khan Mumtaz with a British friend during his studies at the Architectural Association in London in the early 1960s. Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’ The Works in Progress Newsletter Get new articles from Works in Progress delivered to your inbox. Lahore was one of the capitals of the Mughal Empire, and has a vast endowment of historic architecture and urbanism. Mumtaz prepared a seminal report on its historic core, known as the Walled City. This photograph shows the Walled City during the colonial period. Image Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build new, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Image Workers’ houses at Kot Karamat, an early Mumtaz project in the late 1960s. They use a local brick, but also feature arched roofs that are alien to rural Pakistani housing. The workers disliked this, preferring flat roofs where they could sleep on summer nights. Through the 1970s, Mumtaz began to question his approach. ‘I had this growing, nagging fear that I wasn’t communicating with my audience, as a visual artist or as an architect. This grew on me, almost like an obsession.’ In 1980, the Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave him a copy of his book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture. Mumtaz initially paid no attention: ‘Flipping through it, I thought, “Oh yeah, this is traditional Iranian architecture, who cares!” I was totally uninterested.’ But eventually, frustrated by the sense that ‘I didn’t know the language of my own people’, he began to read. ‘From page one, it was mind-blowing. articles.fullContent: Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us.The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the company calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.There is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.The FormulaTake the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of users. That’s it.\[C = \frac{E_{custom}}{\sqrt{U}}\]The square root is important. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a company of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient.Interpreting Your ScoreC < 5Your workspace contains the default emoji set, a company logo, and :party-parrot:, which was added by someone in 2019 who has since left. Nobody uses it any more because it comes across as unprofessional. Communication is conducted exclusively via 👍. People are here for the salary, and they would like you to know that.5 ≤ C < 20A healthy, functional organisation. There is an emoji of the CTO’s face. It is used both supportively and as a weapon, depending on the context.20 ≤ C < 50Thriving. :this-is-fine: has been used over 4,000 times in #incidents. articles.fullContent: Contents Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful. George E. P. Box Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it. So most models carry some uncertainty, whether we chose it or not, and in many decisions it pays to take that uncertainty into account, as the examples in this post show. In my experience, uncertainty in machine learning is a confusing topic to get into, so I wrote this introduction to give an intuitive overview. It is not comprehensive, but it should give you a good enough mental model to choose assumptions that make your uncertainty estimates useful for decision making, even though, as Box put it, the model itself will always be wrong.This post is based on a talk I gave at the University of Alicante. The slides are online. For a more thorough introduction, see Chapters 2 and 3 of my PhD thesis . What Uncertainty Is Generally speaking, uncertainty is incomplete knowledge, and probability is how we describe it: a distribution over the possible outcomes says how plausible each one is, given what we know. It helps to separate two kinds of uncertainty: Epistemic uncertainty comes from what we have not learned yet, such as the true relationship between inputs and outputs. More data can reduce it. Aleatoric uncertainty comes from what we cannot observe: the inputs do not determine the outcome, so more data of the same kind will not remove it. Two kinds of uncertainty. A Gaussian process fit to noisy data. The shaded band is where the model expects the output. Where the aleatoric arrow points, the outputs scatter widely even for similar inputs, so the band stays wide no matter how many points we add. Where the epistemic arrow points, there is no data, so the band is wide because the model does not know the function there, and data there would narrow it. The line between the two depends on what we measure. A coin flip follows classical mechanics. If we do not measure how the coin is thrown, the best we can say is 50/50, and the uncertainty is aleatoric. If we do measure it, physics tells us how it will land, and the uncertainty becomes epistemic: now we have to learn the physics, which takes data. Richer inputs can reduce aleatoric uncertainty, but they give the model more to learn, and whether that pays off depends on how much data and prior knowledge we have.Some inputs are out of reach. For example, weather is chaotic, so tiny differences, as small as the flap of a butterfly's wings, can grow into different weather a few weeks later. Since we cannot observe every butterfly, part of the uncertainty in a forecast stays aleatoric, however much we measure. Why It Matters A prediction is not a decision. When we decide, we often weigh the possible outcomes by how likely they are and what they would cost us, including rare outcomes that could hurt us badly. A single number hides this picture. It also cannot tell us when to hand a case to a human or to collect more data before we decide. The examples below show where modelling uncertainty matters. Five reasons to care about uncertainty. articles.fullContent: Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads. The Problem Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage. The Solution Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time. 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting. Tips Auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed. Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time. Incognito: see the Incognito section above. How It Works Ad detected → Capture timestamp → Reload page → Auto-seek to timestamp → Resume ↓ (if 3 reloads fail) Redirect to yout-ube.com (ad-free mirror, no looping) Two strategies Reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek. yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay issue that the mirror has by default. Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver) Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops Features ✅ Zero ads — reloads until the ad is gone (usually 1-2 cycles) ✅ Timestamp preserved — never lose your place in the video ✅ Live streams — plain reload (no timestamp to preserve) ✅ Ad history database — every ad logged with advertiser, duration, skip text, video, and timestamp ✅ Export — JSON or CSV download of all collected ad data ✅ Popup viewer — click the extension icon to see stats, top advertisers, and full history ✅ No permissions abuse — only storage and tabs, only on YouTube domains Install Option A — Chrome / Brave / Edge / Opera (Load unpacked) Clone the repo: git clone https://github.com/antonpictures/youtube-punisher.git Open chrome://extensions Enable Developer mode (top right) Click Load unpacked → select the youtube-punisher folder Done — activates on all YouTube pages automatically. ✅ Tested Option B — Safari (experimental: AppleScript workaround) Safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher (yt-ad-watch.sh): In Safari, enable: Safari → Settings → Advanced → Show Develop menu in menu bar In Safari (on a YouTube page), run ./yt-ad-watch.sh in Terminal When an ad appears, the watcher detects it via MutationObserver (event-driven in the page), reloads with &t=Xs, and the MutationObserver re-detects on the next page load Note: This is best-effort. As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc. The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own. Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc… These new forks generally all have a few things in common: They focus on a specific subset of models and/or hardware They use a frontier model to vibe-code the entire thing They chase ever-higher token generation speeds … and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model, on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate. In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster. Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. That said, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy. Enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts. It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds. articles.fullContent: Tumblr Likes Calendar Browser extension for Firefox and Chrome that adds a heatmap calendar of your "likes" to the Tumblr Likes page (tumblr.com/likes): each day is shaded based on how many posts you liked, and clicking a day shows the likes from that date right in the panel. Tumblr's likes can't be searched or filtered, so finding an image you saved months ago means scrolling endlessly. This extension turns your likes into something you can actually navigate by date, tag and blog. 📦 Available on Firefox Add-ons: https://addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/tumblr-likes-calendar/ 📦 Available on Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/tumblr-likes-calendar/dhpphdeacendokgoaceccnghjjeineld Features Heatmap calendar of your likes, one panel per year. Click a day → the likes from that day are listed in the panel, without leaving the page. Per-day like count on hover. Tag search: type a tag (or click one of your most-used tags) to list every like carrying it. Blog search: type blog:name, or click a blog name in any result, to list every like from that blog. Gallery of your liked images: a virtualized thumbnail grid that stays fast even with tens of thousands of likes, with an in-place filter by tag or blog:name and a year/month rail to jump straight to any period. Followed blogs tab: indexes the original image posts of the blogs you follow and lets you search them by tag. The download is manual, can cover all blogs or only the ones you pick, and resumes where it stopped. Fast: your data is cached locally after the first scan. Privacy Everything stays on your computer. The extension reads your data through Tumblr's own in-page helper (window.tumblr.apiFetch, no API key needed) and stores your likes (tags, image links, blog, permalink) and the posts downloaded from the blogs you follow only locally, in your browser's IndexedDB. No data is ever sent anywhere. Note that the followed-blogs index can take up hundreds of MB if you download many blogs. How it works The content script runs in the page's main world so it can use window.tumblr.apiFetch, the authenticated helper Tumblr exposes to extensions. It pages through your likes via the API, reads each like's timestamp (likedTimestamp), and groups them by day. Each like is stored in IndexedDB, so subsequent openings are instant and searches by date, tag or blog run locally without calling Tumblr again. Installation The easiest way is to install from the Chrome Web Store or Firefox Add-ons (links above). For Firefox, each GitHub release also includes the signed .xpi file, which you can install directly by opening it in Firefox. From source, for testing: Open Firefox at about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox. Click Load Temporary Add-on…. Select the manifest.json file from this repository. Go to https://www.tumblr.com/likes: a 📅 Likes calendar button appears at the bottom-right. Click it, then press Refresh on first run. Notes and limitations The first scan can take a while if you have many likes. The calendar shows when you liked a post, not when it was published. The number of retrievable likes may be slightly lower than Tumblr's counter: likes on deleted posts or blogs are no longer returned by the API (and are no longer reachable anyway). Requirements Firefox 128 or later, or Chrome 111 or later. Found a bug? Please open an issue on GitHub: https://github.com/Amicolinux/tumblr-likes-calendar/issues — or write to amicolinux@gmx.us. Mention your browser and version, the extension version, and what you did before the problem appeared. Contributing Bug reports and suggestions are welcome via Issues. For changes, feel free to open a Pull Request. License Released under the GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPLv3). See the LICENSE file. Anyone distributing modified versions must keep them open source under the same license.

articles.fullContent: A collection of small, cross-platform, shell-related tools and libraries, in pure Go. charm.land/turtle/coreutils A cross-platform Go implementation of the Unix core utilities. Things like cp, mv, rm, mkdir, chmod and many, many others. See the full list here. import "charm.land/turtle/coreutils/programs/cp" import "charm.land/turtle/coreutils/programs/mv" const workingDir = "" // empty means current // Turtle coreutils has a mini runtime. rt := coreutils.SystemRuntime(workingDir) ctx := context.Background() // Copy! if err := cp.New(rt).Run(ctx, "input.txt", "copy.txt"); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } // Move. if err := mv.New(rt).Run(ctx, "copy.txt", "archive.txt"); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } The goal is not 100% compatibility, but rather to provide a set of small, powerful, flexible tools what work on any platform and architecture supported by go, which can be imported by other Go programs, particularly shell interpreters. Generally compatible with POSIX and GNU Importable Go packages Isolated state (including filesystem) Can run 100% in memory Zero dependencies Pluggable into Go shell interpreters Used by Crush, Task and soon others! Run task bin to compile the binaries locally on ./bin, or import on your Go app like this: go install charm.land/turtle/coreutils@latest Check out pthe full coreutils module](/coreutils/README.md). charm.land/turtle/shcoreutils An mvdan/sh interpreter middleware that resolves core utilities through our coreutils and wires nested command execution back into the interpreter. Particularly useful on platforms where the system utilities are unavailable, like Windows. interpreter, err := interp.New(interp.ExecHandlers(shcoreutils.New())) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } Check out the full docs on the shcoreutils module here. charm.land/turtle/fsx A filesystem abstraction for Go. Built to power the core utilities module, but generic enough to be useful to many other projects. The file system interface from the Go standard library is read-only. This package embeds it and extends it with write-like operations, keeping the read side fully compatible with the stdlib. A superset interface of the Go's standard library's io/fs.FS Extends the stdlib's interface to support write operations like: write, rename, remove, chmod, mkdir and others Default implementations: System (delegates to real FS) Memory FS os.Root wrapper go install charm.land/turtle/fsx@latest fsx.SystemFS(workingDir): use the system's FS fsx.RootFS(root) wraps an os.Root making it compatible with fsx.FS fsx.MemoryFS: an in-memory FS Check out the full docs on the fsx module here. charm.land/turtle/* More comming soon... 👀 Contributing See the contributing guide. Change one line # from pytrends.request import TrendReq from pytrends_cloud import TrendReq pytrends = TrendReq(hl="en-US", tz=360) # reads your APIFY_TOKEN, see below pytrends.build_payload(["python", "javascript", "rust"], timeframe="today 12-m") pytrends.interest_over_time().tail(3) Real output, run on 14 November 2026: python javascript rust isPartial date 2026-10-25 34 4 15 False 2026-11-01 33 4 16 False 2026-11-08 31 4 15 True Install pip install pytrends-cloud Python 3.9 or newer. Dependencies: requests and pandas, like pytrends. Get a token (free) Create a free Apify account: https://console.apify.com/sign-up Copy your API token: https://console.apify.com/settings/integrations Set it once: export APIFY_TOKEN="apify_api_..." # Windows PowerShell: $env:APIFY_TOKEN = "apify_api_..." or pass it directly: TrendReq(apify_token="apify_api_..."). articles.fullContent: A language server for askama templates: completion, hover, go to definition, references, renames, errors and formatting inside templates, from the rust-analyzer you already run. Powers zed-askama a Zed extension. Why I've spent quite a while now playing with non-react stacks out of boredom and curiosity, the one that's stuck for me has been axum/askama/datastar, and I'm working on building up the ecosystem around these things. With a lot of templating alternatives to react, you miss out on the incredible type-safety TSX gives you, and those ergonomics are important to both manual and AI-assisted coding. The stack is pleasant to use, blindingly fast and low-resource-using, solid, and SSR by default. However, being able to drop into templates and edit them kinda sucked as you're effectively blind. No more! With this and the zed extension, you now have full LSP support for symbols, clicking through to stuff, renaming, formatting, and type/error checking using rust-analyzer. Askama compiles a template into Rust inside #[derive(Template)]. rust-analyzer analyses that expansion but cannot map it back to the template, so a broken template shows up as one error on the struct, and the template itself gets no completion or navigation. Existing editor support either highlights only, or approximates askama's code generation by hand and misses whatever the approximation does not cover. askama-analyzer runs askama's own code generator, keeps the template position of every token it generates, and asks rust-analyzer about the result. Answers come back in template positions, and they are the compiler's answers, because the code is the compiler's code. Ecosystem Some projects I've made for the afformentioned stack: askama-analyzer: Language server for askama templates. askama-datastar: Helpers for using Askama with datastar nicely. askama-gettext: Helpers for doing i18 nicely using standardised gettext (po, pot, etc) files. zed-askama: Zed extension to support the LSP with all the bells and whistles. koan-kit-web: An example component library based on Askama and datastar. Installing Each release has archives for macOS (signed and notarised), Linux (static) and Windows, on x86_64 and arm64. Editors Zed: the Askama extension downloads the server and passes it your rust-analyzer settings. Claude Code: editors/claude-code gives Claude Code's LSP tool the server. After each edit to a template, Claude sees askama's and rust-analyzer's errors in it, and it can ask for definitions, references and types there. articles.contentSnippet:
For those who are tracking, Anthropic released an announcement last week about their experimental code mode for Claude Code, claiming some bonkers token savings when it comes to tool calls (95% on some workloads(1)). I haven't benchmarked it myself, but independent studies come in somewhere closer to 60~70% savings (2), but I digress. TLDR; I built an open-source version for the community.
Context: I'm writing an AI RPG engine called Spookery, and I immediately wanted to try this technique for m
articles.fullContent: Ghost Mode Ghost Mode is a Rust library that brings Code Mode to agents. With normal tool calls, every result goes back to the model before it can ask for the next one. Ghost Mode lets the model write a short Python script that chains the calls itself, so intermediate results never go back to the model. Think about it like this: normal tool calling is like going back to the store 30 times to get 30 items. Code Mode is one trip with a shopping list. Say the model needs to know why a pull request's checks failed. Each step needs the one before it. The pull request gives the commit, the commit gives the check runs, and each failed run gives a log. With normal tool calls, that's a round trip to the model per step, and every full result goes through the model. With Ghost Mode, the model sends one script: pr = get_pull_request(number=42) runs = list_check_runs(commit=pr["head_sha"]) failed = [run for run in runs if run["conclusion"] == "failure"] [{"check": run["name"], "log": get_log(run_id=run["id"])[-500:]} for run in failed] The script runs inside your process. The model only gets the last 500 characters of each failed log, not the pull request, every check run, and every full log. Why Ghost Mode Fewer tokens. Anthropic cut one workflow from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 (98.7% less) by having the agent write code against its tools instead of loading every tool definition up front (post). Cloudflare fits its whole API, 2,500+ endpoints, into about 1,000 tokens, where plain MCP tools would take 1.17 million (post). API bills up to 70% lower. Across eight models, code mode cut cost by 70.6% for GPT-5.4 and 40.7% on average (benchmark). Intermediate results never reach the model, so you aren't billed for them as input on every later step. Fewer steps, better results. Models have read way more code than tool-call JSON. Across 17 models, CodeAct's code actions needed up to 30% fewer actions and scored up to 20 points higher success than JSON or text tool calls (paper). Savings depend on the model. In the eight-model benchmark, weaker models retried failed scripts until some runs cost more than plain tool calls, and Gemini models passed fewer tasks. A pre-registered study measured 70% to 90% fewer tokens with three open-weight models. In Ghost Mode, the Limits you build the Sandbox with cap how much any one result can add (40,000 characters by default). Those are other teams' Code Mode numbers. Ghost Mode brings the same idea to Rust. What it takes: give a Sandbox your tools, or point it at an MCP server, and hand the model only two function definitions, execute and poll. The Monty backend runs the script inside your process, so there's no container or extra service. The script can only reach the outside world through your tools. How it works Every arrow inside the caller's process is a plain Rust function call. The model never runs code and only sees the definitions of execute and poll. Writing a host names each part and follows one execute from start to end. Usage Write a host, build a Sandbox, and give the model the execute and poll definitions. When the model calls execute, pass its code to Sandbox::execute and send the Status JSON back. If the run is still going, the model calls poll with the run_id, and you pass that to Sandbox::poll. The crate docs on docs.rs open with a full example: a host with one tool, and a Sandbox that runs one script. Pass Sandbox::tools to schema::mcp_definitions for the pair in MCP shape, or to schema::openai_definitions for OpenAI functions. With the rmcp feature on, pass an mcp::Server to Builder::new instead of writing your own host. Monty, from the monty feature that is on by default, runs the script inside your process and isn't crash-isolated. For untrusted scripts, turn on the monty-pool feature and pass a backend::MontyPool to Builder::new, which runs each session in its own worker process. On Tokio, read Where scripts run first. Sandbox::dump saves an idle session as bytes, and Builder::restore load

The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.

articles.fullContent: Dominic Preston is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.Developers have until February 1st 2027 to declare whether or not they’re a “trader” under UK and European law. Broadly speaking, Google says the definition applies if you earn revenue from your apps, especially if that revenue is regular or at high volume. Developers are exempt if their apps are only a hobby or non-commercial, or if they simply don’t publish them in the UK or Europe.If they self-declare as a trader, developers’ contact details will be shared publicly starting March 1st, including a phone number and address. Google doesn’t accept PO boxes for developer payment profile addresses, meaning many independent developers without an office will either have to share their home address online or pay for a registered agent or other service that provides a business address. One independent developer told The Elec they were considering renting a private office solely to comply with the new rules. We’ve asked Google to confirm why developers aren’t permitted to publish a PO box address, and why details are being shared globally, and will update this article when we hear back.Apple is subject to the same regulations, but is handling them differently to Google. It will only display developer addresses within the relevant European countries, rather than publishing them worldwide. It’s also allowing developers to supply PO box addresses, so long as they provide Apple with a receipt or bill that links the PO box to their regular address.Update, November 26th: Added mention of developers’ option to use a registered agent service for a business address.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Dominic Preston

articles.title: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5
articles.fullContent: Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work. With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos? I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result. A seal dreams of warm sand. Generated entirely on Trainium3. Two goals I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API. For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines. How it works The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened: [ {"name": "dream", "prompt": "Style: cinematic, realistic, shallow depth of field. A plump seal ... is fast asleep on warm golden sand under palm trees ...", "seed": 3}, {"name": "nap", "prompt": "Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... a plump grey seal is fast asleep on a small ice floe ...", "seed": 1, "to": {"shot": "iceberg", "frames": 9}}, {"name": "iceberg", "prompt": "Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... the whole iceberg slowly rolls over ... and washes over the seal. ..."}, {"name": "shake", "prompt": "Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... It slowly shakes its head and body ... and flops down on its belly on the floe, ...", "from": {"shot": "iceberg", "frames": 25}} ] Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next: from: the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion. to: the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it. A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it. Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg. The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal
articles.reason: Analyse concrète de performances d'inférence vidéo et audio avec le modèle LTX-2.5 sur les puces AWS Trainium3.
articles.summary: Hugging Face a pu tester les puces AWS Trainium3 pendant un mois pour exécuter le modèle multimodal LTX-2.5 développé par Lightricks. articles.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
articles.contentSnippet: How $1,500 could qualify every company in the world, why customers hate the model selector, and how Clay is building go-to-market infrastructure for every agent
articles.fullContent: Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue, the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation. By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings. The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows. Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Most companies post-train too early For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks. Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. $1,500 to score every company in the world Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more.
